You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

How to work, in every instance (follow this exactly): keep a program library in the folder /home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1792545366/attempts/c3621f8521cb46cc951a33f146942428/system/state/workspace/programs, one Python file per task, named for its task id (/home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1792545366/attempts/c3621f8521cb46cc951a33f146942428/system/state/workspace/programs/<task id>.py), defining transform(grid), which takes an input grid as a list of lists of integers and returns the output grid.
1. When an instance starts, look for the task's file. If it exists, run its transform on the test input and submit the result before anything else.
2. If there is no file, or its answer was wrong, request demonstration pairs as you judge necessary, write or fix transform, and run it on every pair you have received until it reproduces all of them; then submit its output for the test input. Checking a program on the pairs is free.
3. Submit only grids that your program produced.
4. After the verdict, save the program that reproduced all the pairs to the task's file, replacing any older version, then finish.

---
name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC stream instances using task-id Python programs, demonstrations, and one-action JSON replies.
---

# Continual-ARC

Use for Continual-ARC puzzle instances that require maintaining `programs/<task id>.py` with `transform(grid)`.

1. At instance start, check for the exact task-id file and execute it on the test grid. Submit immediately only if execution succeeds and returns a valid grid; on failure, do not infer a repair from the test grid or traceback. Request a demo before replacing an existing program.
2. When no usable program exists or a submission is incorrect, request demos, then form a rule that explains the examples. Treat each pair as a constraint; run the candidate on every received pair and compare exact grids, dimensions, and orientation before relying on it.
3. Once all pairs match, run the candidate on the test grid, validate its dimensions and cell range, and submit only that program-produced result. If any pair fails, revise the rule before submitting; do not substitute an intuitive visual guess.
4. On every message, put exactly one permitted action JSON object on the final line. After a verdict, save the program that reproduces all available pairs and finish only after re-running the saved version on those pairs.
